“You’ve Got to Be Carefully Taught”: How Apartheid Was Lived and Learned on a South African Farm

Tessa Philips PHD

Tessa Philips

Tessa Philips   Tessa Philips, Ph.D., is a psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice in Sydney, Australia. She is on the faculty of the Sydney University Master of Medicine (Psychotherapy) Program; a Member of the International Council of International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology (IAPSP); and a Board member of the International Association of Relational Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy (IARPP). Suite 709 Harley Place, 251 Oxford Street, Sydney, 2022, NSW, Australia, tessa.philips11@gmail.com

After apartheid ended, many White South Africans asked themselves, over and over, “Who was I during apartheid?” and “How did I learn to live in that way?” This article is an attempt to address those questions. In the first part, a personal example is used to illustrate a life lived during the heyday of apartheid. There was a great silence between the races about race. In the second part, I discuss that life and the nature of embeddedness from a relational, hermeneutic perspective with a self psychological flavor. My doctoral dissertation, titled Race, Place and Self (Philips, 2007), was an attempt to examine the nature and influences over the years of different countries and contexts, and disentangle myself from the particular racialized beginnings that were uniquely mine. This article is one part of that journey.

The Intruder

Michael Larivière PHD

Michael Larivière

Michael Larivière   Michael Larivière, Ph.D. is in Private Practice in Strasbourg, France, and International Seminar Leader (Canada, Italy, United States and Switzerland). 7A Rue Turesine, 6700 Strasbourg, France, michael.julius@orange.fr

“Precocious ability is often nothing more than mimicry,” writes the art connoisseur Brian Sewell (2012) in his memoir, Outsider. This may often be so, but not always, and it certainly wasn’t true of Ferenczi: Mimicry is precisely what he was incapable of, and this may very well be one of the reasons for which Freud was so severe with him.

Role models are the problem; breaking away from them the task. True inventiveness alters what came before, as well as what will follow. Very few names in the history of psychoanalysis are associated with such inventiveness. I can think of four (and I don’t mean here to invite vacuous high gossip; others have certainly mattered but haven’t, I believe, determined analysts; consciousness to the same extent): Freud (of course), Ferenczi, Melanie Klein, and Lacan. So: how Ferenczi?

Long forgotten, he was in France, where I live and work, brought back to the fore by Wladimir Granoff, an analyst born in Strasbourg in 1924 in a family of Jewish Russian immigrants (they had fled Russia after the 1917 revolution). A man of vast culture, fluent in French, Russian, German, and English, he was close to Lacan (until 1964), as well as to the British Middle Group (especially to Winnicott and Masud Khan). It was thanks to Granoff’s efforts that the intruder was let in. Why did Granoff do this? To use the 19th-century historian Michelet’s words, he did this to give the present the new past it called for. And isn’t this, indeed, the very essence of analytical work: to shed new light on a wrinkled, ashen present, a light that can only come from the past, itself forever new? That is what dreams do: They reap all that is repressed during our waking hours. They speak the unspeakable. They weaken the fortified castle of identity and defenses. This is what Ferenczi did as of 1908, incessantly asking what should the analyst say and show, and how, and in what circumstances, of what goes on for him in the analyses he lets himself get involved in.

Ferenczi the intruder, the inspired, Ferenczi who often took the greatest liberties, as well as the greatest risks, with those patients who often were the most seriously affected, Ferenczi the “eccentric”, the “poet of relationships” as Granoff called him, was the one who, like no one else, came to terms with the radical solitude inherent in transference (Lavie 2001). But, this being said, and if truth be told, this capacity for solitude had its source in what Ernest Jones (who had been Ferenczi’s patient, and who deemed him mad) called his “dark side,” and that Granoff sees in the abyss that Ferenczi opened under his contemporaries’ feet by forcing them to acknowledge that theory very often was of no help whatsoever in shedding light on what they were doing (Lavie 2001). 178

Discussion of Ron Bodansky’s Case Presentation

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg   Dr. Lichtenberg is Editor-in-Chief, Psychoanalytic Inquiry Journal. 6256 Clearwood Road, Bethesda, MD 20817, joelichtenberg@aol.com

Dr. Bodansky, hereafter referred to as Ron, asks two interrelated questions. First, what accounts for the ability to improve of a patient who, growing up in an abusive dysfunctional family replete with mental illness, has had a severe deficit of positive or secure attachment experiences? Second, especially given the severity of the troubled background, “How does analysis cure?” That is, what provides the therapeutic leverage to overcome the repetitive downward spiral of dysregulated patterns that form in consequence of a deficit of positive experiences?

Ron speculates: “In her relationship with her father, there was always a hope of a positive attachment and a wish for a bond. Perhaps the hope of mirroring and a small amount of idealization was all that she needed.” I, too, see the father as the key figure, but only to a small degree the father who actually existed—the father who, in contrast to her mother, didn’t beat her; the father who, when she awoke at night with a foot pain, accepted her in his bed and comforted her; the father who repeatedly enacted the role of rescuer only to immediately disappoint. Each of these father–daughter interactions were to play out in the transference—others beat her, Ron didn’t; she could climb on the couch or chair he provided and be comforted when in pain. Ron played the role of rescuer, but was not phony and, rather than disappoint, demonstrated consistency. So what was the source of the sustaining father? I suggest the source lay in her creative potential. The same creative potential allows infants to form a transitional object, some older children to invent an imaginary companion to relieve their loneliness, and all creative writers to activate a theater of the mind, often having some degree of reparative function. But in the face of the regularity of her disappointment with her actual father—himself a traumatized individual—a creative construction could carry but so far. Her mother maliciously interpreted the limitation of her imagination when she told the little girl that the wonderful horse that supported her, and, like a magic carpet, took her wherever she wished to go, was only a verboten dirty stick! The mother later further attacked her creative idealizing of her father by telling the older girl that he had sex with her sister. The sustaining power of an imaginary good father was threatened more directly not only by his disappointing actions, but also, even more important, by his failure to protect her from her mother and from other destructiveness within the family. Andrea Harms

Andrea Harms   Andrea Harms, Ph.D., is a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst in private practice in Vienna and Gmunden, Austria. She is training analyst, supervisor and director of the “Vienna Circle for Psychoanalysis and Self Psychology” (WKPS) and a member of the International Council for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology. Schiffnerstr. 16/2, 4810, Gmunden, Austria, a.harms@utanet.at

In this article, I discuss Ron Bodansky’s presentation (this issue), “Release from Developmental Arrest,” from a Viennese perspective. Vienna, Kohut’s birthplace, the town in which he spent his childhood and adolescence, where he studied and had his first analysis with August Aichhorn, was the place to establish the first Self Psychological Training Institute in Europe: the Vienna Circle for Psychoanalysis and Self Psychology, a state recognized Training Institute, founded in 1987.

Which direction has Self Psychology been taking in Austria since then? We began with the exploration of self-structure, moved via empathy to a focus on selfobject experiences and then many of us joined in the appreciation of the importance of intersubjectivity theory. My discussion reflects this particular theoretical orientation, an orientation that makes the attempt to observe and understand both the ongoing process of mutual influence that is at the heart of intersubjectivity theory, as well as the self object needs and transferences that become mobilized in the patient within this process.

Patients regularly make demands for responses that go beyond listening and nonjudgmental exploration. This article proposes a conceptual framework that allows inquiry into spontaneously emerging positive enactments as a clinical resource.

The Primary Processes: A Preliminary Exploration of A-Rational Mentation from an Evolutionary Viewpoint

Susan Cutler PHD and Linda Brakel MD

Linda Brakel

Linda Brakel   Dr. Brakel is Associate Professor (adj), Department of Psychiatry, University of Michigan; Research Associate, Department of Philosophy, University of Michigan; and Faculty Member, Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.525 Third Street 21-E, Ann Arbor, MI 48103. brakel@umich.edu

In this article we investigate research on nonhuman animal cognition revealing the predominance of primary processes-like operations that are effective and adaptive from an evolutionary perspective. But first and from a different direction, we review a body of recently popular empirical work on human heuristics and biases that proposes System 1 and System 2 as a dual-process model of cognition and emotion; this without acknowledging Freud’s primary and secondary processes. Thus, we explore the parallels between primary process and System 1, as we evaluate the case for the evolutionary nature of primary process. We guide the reader through literature on animal cognition and that of System 1 biases and heuristics to provide the psychoanalytic reader with the opportunity to make important links to psychoanalytic concepts.

An Intimate Success With Veronica

Susan Flinders PHD

Susan Flinders

Susan Flinders   Dr. Flinders is Graduate of Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute; Adjunct Faculty, Michigan State University Osteopathic Medicine; Adjunct Faculty, Madonna University; and in private practice in Commerce Township and Chelsea, Michigan. 19700 Waterloo Road, Chelsea, MI 48118, slfphd@aol.com

In this aricle, I address how intimacy, intrapersonally (trait) and interpersonally (state) contains the therapeutic action in an analysis of a traumatized woman named Veronica. The article summarizes the psychoanalytic literature related to the concept of intimacy. I discuss briefly how empathy, despite the analyst’s focus on its presence in the analysis, is not the key to the successful analysis. I then detail how intimacy, in its various forms, helps the analysis succeed despite the seeming distress of the patient and even sometimes that of the analyst.

Arnold Rachman Ph.D., F.A.G.P.A.

Arnold Rachman

Arnold Rachman   Arnold Wm. Rachman, Ph.D., F.A.G.P.A. is a Training and Supervising Analyst; Faculty member at The Institute of the Postgrad Psychoanalytic Society, New York City; Clinical Professor of Psychology at Derner Institute; Adelphi Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis & Psychotherapy, Garden City, NY; and on the Board of Directors at Sándor Ferenczi Study Center, The New School for Social Research, New York City. 8777 Collins Avenue, No. 210 Surfside, FL 33154 arnold.rachman@gmail.com

I have had a long and difficult intellectual, emotional, and interpersonal struggle in becoming a psychoanalyst. For the first fourteen years of my analytic career, I did not have an exemplar in psychoanalysis with whom to identity until I discovered Sándor Ferenczi in 1978, fourteen years after I began training at what was then Postgraduate Center for Mental Health, in New City.

My academic and personal experiences prior to analytic training had made a significant positive contribution to my identity. As I look back over my preanalytic experience, there were teachers, supervisors, and colleagues that provided me with the necessary affirmation to pursue the study of psychology and psychotherapy. At University of Buffalo, as an undergraduate, Olive Lester, the Chairperson of the Psychology Department, directly expressed her feelings to me that I had the ability to become a psychologist and should pursue graduate studies. Walter Gruen and Aron Hershkovitz had faith in my capacity to become a clinician. Marvin Farber, a student of the philosopher Edmund Husserl, the founder of phenomenology, taught me to appreciate logic and the scientific method and the importance of phenomenology.

I was also influenced by my training in humanistic psychology at The Counseling and Psychotherapy Research Center at The University of Chicago, founded by Carl Rogers. At The Counseling Center, Robert Butler, Rosalyn Cartwright, Eugene Gendlin, Laura Rice, John Shlien, and Fred Zimring showed me respect by treating me as a young colleague, not an ignorant beginner. Teaching at The Counseling Center emphasized intellectual liberalism, American empiricism, empathy, flexibility, and responsiveness in clinical functioning. These client-centered psychotherapists never acted like they possessed the truth. Intellectually, they taught me to search for a truth by developing hypotheses and collecting data. One was to use the phenomenological method of attuning to the actual immediate experience in the clinical interaction to determine whether to accept or reject one’s hypotheses (Rachman 2006a, 2006b, 2007, 2011).

Mauricio Cortina MD and Giovanni Liotti MD

Giovanni Liotti

Giovanni Liotti   Dr. Liotti is a member of APC School of Psychotherapy, Rome, Italy.Giovanni Liotti, M.D. Viale Castro Pretorio 116 00185, Rome Italy. gio.liotti@fastwebnet.it

A taxonomy of basic motivational systems (reptilian, mammalian, and neo-mammalian), that emerged in phases during the course of millions of years, is proposed. These different phases did not replace each other, but became reorganized in the brain at different hierarchical levels. It is argued that (a) humans are an ultracooperative species and (b) high degrees of cooperation put strong selective pressures toward the development of sophisticated forms of intersubjective communication. These two developments had cascading effects on human evolution, creating both the conditions upon which humans were able to understand intentions, gestures, emotions, and, ultimately, the minds of others, and the emergence of language and symbolic forms of cultural evolution. Possible evolutionary steps that led to this ultracooperative survival strategy and some of their genetic mechanism, with special emphasis on a multilevel model of selection, are described, and the implications for psychotherapy and psychoanalysis are explored.

I. I. FREUD’S CONCEPT OF “WILD ANALYSIS”

In his paper, “Observations on Wild Psychoanalysis,” Freud (1910) succinctly outlined the issue of technical errors that can cause harm to a patient. He described a young physician eager to apply the insights of the new science of psychoanalysis to the treatment of a middle-age woman suffering from intense anxiety. This physician gave the woman a premature interpretation. He interpreted her anxiety as due to her frustrated sexual desires because she was divorced from her husband and lacked sexual contact and satisfaction. Her anxiety mounted, rather than diminished, as the result of this premature interpretation.The physician sent the patient to Freud to verify what he considered a correct interpretation. Freud used this consultation to develop the concept of wild analysis, the inappropriate use of psychoanalytic theory that did not take into account the clinical concepts of resistance, repression, and relationship, which are necessary in the psychoanalysis of a neurosis.

These developments were considered regressive deviations and were labeled not psychoanalysis by the traditionalists (Rachman 1997a, 1997b, 2003b).

Arnold Rachman Ph.D., F.A.G.P.A.

Arnold Rachman

Arnold Rachman  

The contributions to this Ferenczi issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry have demonstrated the contemporary expansion of Ferenczi scholarship. Since the last Ferenczi issue in 1997, it is no longer a matter of trying to reestablish Ferenczi’s forgotten legacy for psychoanalysis to which the 1997 issue contributed. Then, barely 10 years after the English publication of Ferenczi’s landmark Clinical Diary (Ferenczi 1988), Ferenczi scholarship was dominated by European analysts as the 1997 issue demonstrated. Now, 15 years later, I was able to include five contributions from the United States, which indicates that Ferenczi scholarship is now part of American psychoanalysis.

What is also of interest is the shift from historical inquires to the application of Ferenczi’s ideas to contemporary theory and technique in psychoanalysis. Leading the way in contemporary analysis is the integration of Ferenczi’s ideas in his confusion of tongues paradigm and the issue of trauma. Eva Papiasvili, Robert Prince, Arnold Wm. Rachman, and Mr. M. W. address the basic issue of trauma. It can now be seen as a distinct psychological disorder that can be integrated into an analytic perspective. The confusion of tongues paradigm is very meaningful in both understanding trauma disorders and in analyzing them. This new positive direction in contemporary psychoanalysis is a significant change from the period when Ferenczi first introduced the confusion of tongues in 1933. Then the paper and Ferenczi were rejected and ridiculed by the traditional analytic community. The study and treatment of trauma that Ferenczi pioneered is now alive and well in Europe and the United States. When society and psychoanalysis become open to returning to its origins and rediscover the study of the incest trauma, Ferenczi’s work will be ready to contribute. This issue attempts to contribute to this evolutionary step in psychoanalysis.

Arnold Wm. Rachman, Ph.D., F.A.G.P.A.

John Launer MD

John Launer

John Launer   Dr. Launer is a family and couple psychotherapist and an honorary consultant at the Tavistock Clinic, London. He is associate dean for postgraduate medical education at London University.79 Stanhope Avenue, London N3 3LY, United Kingdom. johnlauner@aol.com

In this article, I first offer a summary of Darwin’s main ideas, especially relating to sex, and explain how these have been elaborated by more recent evolutionary scholars. I then give an account of the historical divergence between psychoanalysis and classical Darwinian thought, and describe how the early psychoanalyst Sabina Spielrein tried to counter this by addressing some biological themes in her work. Following a review of some contemporary attempts to bring psychoanalysis and evolutionary thought into alignment with each other, I make some suggestions regarding a view of sex and sexuality that would be sound in evolutionary terms while also being helpful in psychoanalytic ones.

In this article, I propose to accept “interminability” as a legitimate need of the patient, unlike the tendency to treat it as a problem or as a negative phenomenon indicating an unsuccessful therapy. I present clinical vignettes demonstrating how some patients require a therapist for an unlimited time, continuously or at intervals. These patients require the therapeutic secure base and do not aspire—nor should they be encouraged—to terminate therapy. From the empathic stance of self psychology, such prolonged needs may be respected and provided.

Prologue: How Do We Explain Psychoanalytic Improvement in Patients Who Have Been Highly Traumatized: An Exploration of Therapeutic Action in Psychoanalysis: Part I

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Understanding the place of reality in the psychoanalytic relationship has been a vexing problem since Freud conceptualized that the cause of psychopathology was not traumatic events like sexual abuse that were generated in reality, but within the patient’s mind as fantasies. This proposition led to the exploration of the patient’s inner world and psychoanalysis as we know it was born.

Yet Freud, and almost every other analyst, was never satisfied with this explanation because, although fantasy is integral to psychopathology, the patient’s experiences of external reality in the present and past find their way into psychopathology and could not be ignored; there was both nature and nurture to consider, especially in the clinical situation where, for the patient, the external reality of the analyst was ever present. The problem is best seen in the difficulty over where to place trauma within the mind. When examining the mind in the analytic relationship the only actual reality is within the relationship between the patient and analyst in the present moment, the experience of many past realities are also expressed in the present moment. Memories of trauma become one of those difficult past realities which in the clinical situation is intra psychic and part of a repetition, i.e., the patient experiences the repetition of the trauma as if it is a new event and it is through the therapeutic action of an analysis that true change is possible.

In no other analytic situation can one follow as well the distortions of reality because of trauma as it appears in transferences, resistances, and repetition of severely traumatized patients because the experience of a trauma can be unbearable and the distortion of reality, which contributes to psychopathology is life saving.

With this in mind, we have planned two issues devoted to the question of how we explain psychoanalytic improvement in patients with severe psychopathology. Each of the next two issues will begin with a description of an analysis of a patient with severe personality disorder that was presented at the International Association of Self Psychology Conference in 2010. The contributors to the issues will present original articles based upon the reflections of the analysis. The ideas that evolve from the articles add to their understanding of the psychopathology of highly traumatized patients, their improvement, the place of reality in their treatments and lives, and finally improving our understanding of clinical psychoanalysis in general.

Who is the Hero in the Life of the Traumatized Patient? Reflections on Bodansky’s Work with Mrs. E

Michael Shulman PHD

Michael Shulman

Michael Shulman   Dr. Shulman is on the Faculties of Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute and University of Michigan (Psychiatry), and in private practice of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy in Ann Arbor, Michigan. 117 N. First Street, Suite 113, Ann Arbor, MI 48104, mshulmanphd@gmail.com

The vexed question of how to explain analytic success with traumatized patients like Bodansky’s Mrs. E is considered from a perspective on psychoanalytic history and the specific theory-buttressed assumptions and practices of earlier generations of analysts that led them to conclude that traumatized patients couldn’t be helped via psychoanalytic work. I then consider Mrs. E’s life with an organizing question, Who is its hero?, applying perspectives from Charles Dickens and from Fraiberg and colleagues’ work, and use these perspectives to question the theory-based assumption that Mrs. E must have somewhere had a good object experience to have a life. These perspectives allow contemplation of a saving forceful agency at Mrs. E’s core (perhaps one experienced by her as “animal”) that seems essential to understanding her successes in living. The success of her treatment in assisting her with building a life suggests that her analyst’s helping her with mirroring and, even more important, with mentalizing, contribute importantly to her life improvement. Some potential limitations of his approach to her are also implied in his account; in particular, his limited work with her intimate desires and feelings, both libidinal and aggressive.

The Paradox of Holding and Recognizing and the Local Moving Along of the Therapeutic Process

Susanna Federici-Nebbiosi PHD

Susanna Federici-Nebbiosi

Susanna Federici-Nebbiosi  

In an attempt to provide a first incomplete answer to the question raised by the editors as to “what cures traumatized patients,” I join my voice to that of the many authors who associate therapeutic action with the process of affect regulation that develops within the analytic dyad. I believe that we are yet to find effective ways of describing the therapeutic process so that the fundamental elements can be reflected upon and studied by therapists. This is especially important when we are working with severely traumatized patients. One of the challenges we are facing today has to do with the way in which therapists communicate such experiences to each other. In our reflections, it all depends on the level at which we situate ourselves, if the therapist places himself/herself at the local level of the interactive process he/she needs to learn to stand in the uncertainty of the security and change paradox relying on the intersubjective process itself. With traumatized patients the challenge in psychotherapy almost always involves the ‘treatment that hurts’ paradox.

Epilogue: How Do We Explain Psychoanalytic Improvement in Patients Who Have Been Highly Traumatized: An Exploration of Therapeutic Action in Psychoanalysis: Part I

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

The authors’ efforts at reaching the humanity within the analysis of Mrs. E and to find explanations that will address her evolving personhood are themes that exists in all the articles of this issue. In my prologue, I described that attention in an analytic relationship to patients who have been severely traumatized brings up the difficulty that they have had in embracing reality; the reality of themselves who are developing human beings as they try to find their voices and the reality that surrounds them where boundaries are actually distinct, but for them are dramatically distorted because of the disruptive intensity of their inner lives and difficulty in dealing with such disruptive intensity. Because of the analytic relationship, significant changes take place that lead to more coherence in the way patients deal with their inner lives including their experiences of reality.

The analytic relationship becomes an excellent setting to follow the transformations from a distorted to a more coherent view of themselves and the external world. A major stumbling block that analysts have had is their attempt to be true to Freud’s model, where he understood reality to be simply outside of the patient. Patients knew reality as a result of cognition and perception of the external world without going into the depths of the mind. He placed little attention to what is it like to be a whole person, an “I” who doesn’t simply perceive reality, but creates reality with the use of everything that is inside and registered from the outside. A whole person experiences himself as having value, as an agency with vitality, ideals, direction and capacities of self-reflection and reflexivity; by reflexivity I mean to feel like a whole person who is able to work with thoughts and feelings that lead to transformations and creativity. Without a useable concept of wholeness in the analytic relationship, the analyst is frequently left with only parts of the whole in analyzing patients. Frequently in the analysis of patients who have been severely traumatized, their symptoms rest on how they do not experience themselves as a whole people who are fully alive, able to feel close or feel at all. As a result of their trauma, they frequently find hiding their wholeness enables them to survive.

Prologue: How Do We Explain Psychoanalytic Improvement in Patients Who Have Been Highly Traumatized: An Exploration of Therapeutic Action in Psychoanalysis: Part II

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

In the Prologue that I wrote for the first issue of “How Do We Explain Psychoanalytic Improvement in Patients Who Have Been Highly Traumatized: An Exploration of Therapeutic Action in Psychoanalysis,” I described that the place of reality in the analytic relationship is especially important when dealing with patients whose ability to deal with reality is seriously compromised. In the analytic relationship, one should be able to follow the nature of dynamic transformations where pathological and nonpathological perceptions of reality that become central to the material are expressed and played out with the analyst.

In the Epilogue of that issue, I wrote that each author of the articles in the issue emphasized that the approach to the patient that led to success in the treatment was based on Ron Bodansky’s ability to reach the humanity and wholeness of Mrs. E, so that she could experience the safety of being human, which included the recognition of her enormously traumatic experience that contributed to her identity. Ron Bodansky was able to do this because he was able to avoid remaining in the abyss of the patient’s defensive regressive withdrawal from the reality of the present moment that had made her life so difficult; instead he provided her with a new experience of his entering the abyss with her and recovering from it as he empathized and reached out to her in the intensity of the reality of the analytic interchange.

In this second issue, Paolo Stramba-Badiale describes an analysis that he conducted with a highly traumatized woman, Veronica. The articles and discussion in this issue enable the reader to deepen further the understanding of how to explain analytic improvement in patients who have been highly traumatized. Reading the articles in this issue takes one beyond the safety and empathy that was discussed in the first issue. The theme that appears repeatedly in this issue is that the analyst must join the patient in bearing her suffering and then help the patient find a way to live with the suffering by working to transform it into a narrative that leads to joy and freedom.

Discussion on “Affective Attunement, Vulnerability, Empathy: The Analytic Experience With Veronica” by Paolo Stramba-Badiale

Alan Kindler MD

Alan Kindler

Alan Kindler   Dr. Kindler is Past President and Faculty, Institute for the Advancement of Self Psychology, Toronto; Faculty, Toronto Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis; Training and Supervising Analyst, Toronto Institute of Psychoanalysis; Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, University of Toronto School of Medicine. 49 Jackman Avenue, Toronto, Ontario M4K 2X5, Canada, kindler@ca.inter.net

Paolo has shared a moving account of the 8-year analysis of Veronica, which went remarkably well. One sees, by the end, significant gains for this very disturbed and dysfunctional young woman who, at the age of 30, dared yet again to risk repeating the traumatic relational events of her life in what must have been a faint hope for a new beginning. His vivid descriptions of some of the excruciating events of Veronica’s life, including her previous failed attempts at group and individual psychoanalytic therapy, allow readers to enter into the helpful relationship they established, despite the difficulties between them, through the years they spent working together. Paulo’s rich account permits readers to witness the almost impossible problems that a traumatized person can bring to the analytic relationship, struggling as they do to stay at times intact, at times fragmented and at times, some combination of both.

From the outset, Paulo saw Veronica as “a frightened person with little control over her feelings” and noted that her affect was often disconnected from the painful experiences she was describing; “she would speak in a particular tone of voice, which contrasted with the description of her unease” (p. 280). In other words, her simulated serenity masked her dissociated turmoil and despair.

I agree with Paulo’s formulation of Veronica’s difficulties in terms of self-regulatory problems associated with her tendency to dissociate from those parts of her self that, for various reasons, had been rendered unacceptable in many relational contexts. From the beginning, it seems clear that her anguished and injured self states might be among those unacceptable areas of her subjective world. Her profoundly limited, and therefore ineffective, access to her own emotional pain renders her an extremely vulnerable person who found herself constantly in grossly unsuitable, even harmful, relationships. Conceptually, one might say that competent aversiveness is fundamental to competent attachment, and competent aversiveness, in turn, requires unfettered access to both the experience of, and the expression of, distress. All were profoundly lacking for Veronica, thereby contributing to her disastrous relationships.

Effective Therapeutic Action During Paolo Stramba-Badiale’s Analytic Experience With Veronica

Richard Hertel PHD

Richard Hertel

Richard Hertel   Dr. Richard K. Hertel is a Faculty member at the University of Michigan School of Medicine, Department of Psychiatry and Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute. 505 E. Huron Street Ann Arbor, MI 48104, rkhertel@umich.edu

Veronica, a 39-year-old woman, struggled with severe attachment anxiety stemming from frequent attachment trauma episodes throughout her life. She presented with problems in affect regulation, object and self constancy, and reality testing. She relied heavily on primitive concrete modes of thinking, and struggled with overwhelming shame and guilt, seeking their expiation in sadomasochistic relationships. Dr. Stramba-Badiale’s exquisite, intrepid use of self analysis enabled him to contain Veronica’s nonverbal, as well as verbal, primitive affects and enabled a co-created therapeutic alliance sufficiently safe to analyze the primitive horrors in her relationships with mother, father, sisters, and husband. This eventuated in marked improvement in affect regulation, object and self constancy, a sense of herself as a good enough mother deserving good for herself and her daughter. Notably, there was no mention of any sexual or triadic aspects in her object relationships.

Epilogue: How Do You Explain Psychoanalytic Improvement in Patients Who Have Been Highly Traumatized: An Exploration of Therapeutic Action in Psychoanalysis: Part II

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Upon studying the two issues, I have developed a model of successful analysis of a highly traumatized patient that begins with my entering the experiences of two whole people, the patient and analyst. The patient is expressing facets of chronic trauma that are dissociated and repressed. As a result of the dissociation and repression, she is without an experience of agency or ownership of the facets of her chronic trauma. She feels hopeless in taking any ownership that would bring her closer to transforming the facets of her trauma into her narrative with a greater appreciation of what she has lived through in the context of her living today. As the trauma is repeated, she feels helpless, powerless, and unable to control her affects in a state of being injured while being unable to be reached by empathy. To even try to communicate her trauma fills her with defeat and generates unbearable humiliation. The most pressing question for the patient in her analysis is: How can I go on living in the present moment if I am unable to elevate my trauma into a more organized “consciousness?”

In the clinical situation, there is an intersubjective partnership toward making coherence from the dissociated and repressed parts of the patient. For the analyst, she becomes emotional, immersed in the patient’s trauma with a replica of her own trauma. In this state, she works toward bringing coherence and a narrative out of her patient’s experience by promoting a relationship that is safe while doing work of reaching out with interpretations. The safe relationship immersed with interpretations demonstrates that one can feel safe and work toward understanding the past from the present by baring the vulnerability of it all.

In my Prologue of the first issue, I said that an exploration of highly traumatized patients in a successful analysis should bring clarity of the place of reality in the analytic situation. In the patient’s experience, we see a gross distortion because, in the past, reality was too much to handle. In the context of the present moment of the analysis, the patient enters a slow process of gaining emotional strength by working at integrating the trauma, resulting in emotional freedom and an increased well being. Empathy is the mainstay of the analytic process, but not without the emotional work of the patient and analyst.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue: Never Ever Stop Learning More About Supervision

Imre Szecsödy MD

Imre Szecsödy

Imre Szecsödy  

Psychoanalytic training was institutionalised 1922 at the Berlin Congress. It was built on the tripartite model: personal analysis as the basis, to get in touch with the method as well as with the influence of the unconscious on everyday as well as professional life; didactic training to learn the theory; and supervision to integrate the experience and theory with the candidate’s personality. It is essential to emphasize that as soon as training becomes organized, it poses trainer and trainees with many problems, such as: What should be the content of a training program; who should be selected for such training, and by whom and according to what kinds of principles; and, last but not least, how is one to find the most productive teaching methods? It is also important to stress that the syncretism of the psychoanalytic education is the problematic combination of roles and functions. The task of the institute is both to educate and cure the trainee. The trainee is thus a pedagogic unit or object of teaching and a therapeutic unit or object of psychoanalytic procedure. The administrator-teacher syncretism places the student in a regression producing infantilizing position.

There are still many different opinions about how to select candidates and organize the curriculum and length of training. To define psychoanalytic talent is difficult; the uncertainty to determine what criteria to use for selection is great. The problematic overlap between personal analysis and training is constantly present. It is also interesting and intriguing that supervision, which is used at all training institutions, is hardly questioned in regard to its usefulness. There are only a few studies about the so-called ill effects of supervision. Training is considered by many to be mainly a process of personal development. In most psychoanalytic institutes, senior analysts, who have gained recognition for their theoretical papers, for their lecturing, or for their large analytic practices, become training analysts, which gives them the status and the right to have candidates in training analysis. To work as supervisors follows more or less automatically from this status. Pedagogic competence was neither emphasised nor acknowledged as a prerequisite for working as a supervisor. This may be due to an idealization of analytic work and based on the idea that because one has gained an understanding of, and skill for, the work as such, one has also acquired the capacity to convey this knowledge and skill to others and to facilitate its acquisition by them.1 This idea is also mirrored in the large amount of literature, written anecdotically about supervision, expressing more or less individual and idiosyncratic views as generally valid observations. Even studies that more systematically investigate the supervisory work focus on how one teaches, and less on how one learns in supervision.

Epilogue: Never Ever Stop Learning More About Supervision

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

During the last century, there has been a revolution in the canons of science that began with the Enlightenment that promised the laws of the universe could be understood with objectivity and rationality; that reality was static, concrete, and could be reached, studied, and validated to something far more relative where the objective and subjective virtually merge while reality is continually developing and evolving.

Objectivity and subjectivity comprise the infrastructure of psychoanalysis; both perspectives are always present. They are separated only in psychoanalytic theories and when these theories are awkwardly applied to the clinical and the teaching situations. An example of this is the theoretical approach of neutrality and the objective stance of the analyst to free associations, which has created conservable confusion and misunderstanding while clinically creating needless suffering.

This entire issue is devoted to filling an enormous gap in the understanding and teaching of supervision, which has been encumbered by old simplistic ideas of supervision: If you understand analysis, you can supervise. Each article has contributed to illuminating the needed ideas and approaches to promulgate more contemporary psychoanalytic ideas and techniques.

In his discussion, Cláudio Laks Eizirik (this issue) wrote “As in so many fields of human activity, there are a few persons who embrace an idea, a cause, an ideology, a mission, and dedicate the best of their efforts to bring more light, or effectiveness to this cause; international psychoanalysis owes to Imre [Szecsödy] and his work a more clear objective and research-oriented view on the fascinating activity that is psychoanalytic supervision” (p. 642). The quotation conveys the essence of this issue that is embodied in its title, “Never Ever Stop Learning More About Supervision.”

Melvin Bornstein, M.D.

Issue Editor

Epilogue: Analytic Lives in a Wounded World

Doris Brothers PHD

Doris Brothers

Doris Brothers  

What made us choose to become psychoanalysts? How did we come to devote our working lives to healing the emotional suffering of our fellow humans? What drew us to the psychoanalytic theories that guide our work? The articles and discussions in this issue should dispel all doubt that we could even begin to answer these questions without reflecting on our place in the world.

Not only have my fellow contributors provided intimate glimpses into their development as analysts and as human beings, they have also opened portals into our world that might otherwise have remained inaccessible. Much of what they courageously revealed involves the darkest aspects of human relatedness and documents the grievous harm we are capable of inflicting on one another. At the same time, they have shown us what is most inspiring about our shared humanity. In light of what they have risked letting us know, perhaps we can dare to hope that healing is possible not only for our patients, but also for ourselves and those with whom we share our planet.

I cannot find words to express my profound gratitude for these extraordinary contributions.

Doris Brothers, Ph.D.

Issue Editor

Epilogue: Psychoanalysis and Evolution: The Tentative Connection

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

In the prologue I wrote that because of advances in psychoanalysis, sociobiology, and evolution, there is a positioning in each of these areas of knowledge for a greater integration to enrich our understanding of human life. The six articles attest to this. Some of the theoretical formulations in psychoanalysis and cognitive psychology require alteration to the current state of knowledge (Cutler and Brakel, and Modell). The data needed to advance understanding of the development of subjectivity requires a plurality of theoretical and conceptual approaches (Hobson, Launer, Carlton and Shane).

Sexuality bridged by evolutionary principles remains essential to an understanding of body and mind in human and animal life (Launer).

Insights from the advances in anthropology, sociobiology and psychoanalysis reveal that similar theoretical and clinical models have explanatory power in their application to two very different fields of study, the brain and mind in primates and humans (Cortina and Liotti, and Carlton and Shane, and Hobson).

The explorations of the qualities of caring and cooperation that contribute to one’s humanity leaves much to understand, especially whether there is a distinct place for true caring and cooperation apart from reciprocal altruism; i.e., tit for tat.

Melvin Bornstein, M.D.

Issue Editor

In this article we consider Nobel Prize Winner Gerald Edelman’s remarkable contribution to the understanding of human evolution, and our own application of Edelman’s theory to a brain-based psychoanalytic perspective we have devised. Edelman’s paradigm setting out his theory of the evolution of mind, brain, and consciousness concerns not only mankind’s evolution over all of time, but also the evolution of each and every individual over and within his single lifetime. Edelman contends that human beings, as individuals, and not only as the taxonomic category from which they sprang, have a separate and distinct evolutionary history of their own, and it is especially from within Edelman’s theoretical assumptions about the evolution of the individual per se that our own psychoanalytic understanding of theory and practice derives.

In this discussion, I consider two substantially different articles about growing up in South Africa and the authors’ reflections on how this has influenced them. I focus on two issues raised by both Straker and Philips: that of becoming conscious of what Straker, drawing on the work of Ngai (2003), describes as ugly emotions, and the issue of voice—who can speak, who cannot, and some of the complexities that surround this issue. I refer to the problematic fact that the three voices heard in this section on South Africa are White and that each one of us has benefitted markedly from apartheid. I make reference to the power of knowledge and the potentially transformative nature of the voices that speak it as is evidenced in both articles. However, I draw attention to the fact that the knowledge and the voices that speak it have not actually done much to change the status quo in current day South Africa—inequality, poverty, marginalization, and oppression continue to be reproduced and maintained. Referring to the emotional struggles that come with this consciousness on a daily basis, I conclude with a hope, nevertheless, that a tiny bit of growth and transformation might usefully come from what each of us has attempted to say in these articles.

Annette Richard

Annette Richard   Annette Richard, M.Ps., is Chair and Co-Founder of the Groupe d’Étude sur l’Intersubjectivité, a Montréal affiliate of the International Association for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology. Although attachment patterns and early relational interactions are very important in creating implicit and procedural memories, I contend, along with many authors (Gentile, 2010; Sucharov, 2012), that the historical, cultural, political, and social contexts give them meanings. Grounding myself in a relational systems theory of trauma and therapeutic healing (Brothers, 2008), I attempt to capture how a historic traumatic event in my ancestors’ lives, the Acadian Deportation, has shaped and affected my life and work as a therapist. Different themes and meanings—for example, submission and surrender (Ghent, 1990), autonomy and liberation, and restorative efforts in the aftermath of trauma that involve the reduction of complexity (Brothers, 2008)—will be revealed as part of the legacy of the historical traumatic exile and return of my Acadian ancestors. After briefly describing the tragic history of the Acadian people, I retrace my own initiatory, and never completed, journey back home as an Acadian woman therapist, through traumatic submission and its active counterpart, the impulse to dominate. A brief vignette from my work with a patient serves to illustrate how my Acadian heritage is still an active and conflictual process for me.

This article highlights the issue of how the practice of psychoanalytic therapy is affected by its being conducted within the context of war and terror. The author confides not having given this question any systematic thought prior to writing the article, in spite of having lived and worked for decades in that context. He shows how his personal history and the course of his career as a therapist were intertwined with the history of the political conflict, and politically involved though he was, he seems to have vertically split-off its potential effect on his therapeutic work. This section of the issue was suggested by Joe Lichtenberg, M.D., Editor-in-Chief of Psychoanalytic Inquiry when we discussed the potential contributions for this Ferenczi issue. Joe said, “Why don’t you include an article about how Ferenczi has influenced the practice of contemporary analysts?” As soon as we heard this suggestion, we knew it was a great idea. Ferenczi’s dissident ideas and methods have had enduring appeal to a group of psychoanalysts since their introduction eighty-seven years ago, in spite of deliberate attempts to suppress, criticize, ignore, or present personal and political attacks on his functioning (Rachman 1997a, 1997b, 1999).

Since then, Ferenczi’s work has been translated into French, English, Italian, and Spanish. A devoted group of American, European, and Latin psychoanalysts have demonstrated the significance of Ferenczi’s lost legacy for psychoanalysts. The enduring interest in Ferenczi’s ideas to this group of devoted followers, we believe, is due to an emotional connection to the drama of his life, career and to expression of his personality. Our contributors were asked to discuss their personal reactions to Ferenczi’s work and how they informed their clinical work.

Susan Klett outlined the contributions that Ferenczi’s work has made to her work with difficult cases, the kind to which Ferenczi had originally devoted his clinical focus. In particular, Klett believes that Ferenczi’s groundbreaking paper, “The Confusion of Tongues” (Ferenczi 1980), is crucial in her analysis of difficult cases. Ferenczi’s paper provided the emotional, as well as the intellectual, impetus to provide the therapeutic atmosphere necessary.

Michael Larivière, an analyst working in Strasbourg, France, described contributions that Ferenczi made to his personal analysis through the influence of Ferenczian analyst in France. He is grateful to him for following in Ferenczi’s footsteps by being a responsive not a withholding analyst.

Mr. M. W. is an analysand of Arnold Wm. Rachman, who is self-taught student of psychoanalysis. When he expressed an interest in Ferenczi, he was given Ferenczi’s “The Confusion of Tongues” (1980) paper, which addressed his own basic issue of childhood trauma. Mr. M. W. found “The Confusion of Tongues” paper emotional moving.

Arnold Modell MD

Arnold Modell

Arnold Modell   Dr. Modell is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School; and Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute.82 Kirkstall Road Newtonville, MA 02460. amodell617@aol.com

Freud’s Lamarckian beliefs contributed to his theory of instincts, as well as his concepts regarding the unconscious primary process. Freud’s theory of the primary and secondary process is fundamentally biological, as he placed it within an evolutionary context and hypothesized that the two systems were distinguished by free and bound psychic energy. Freud’s distinction between the primary and secondary process is one of the few psychoanalytic theories that has been confirmed by science. We believe that Freud was correct in maintaining that the primary process is of earlier evolutionary origin than the secondary process. But Freud failed to recognize the distinction between primary-process thinking that occurs in dreams and that which occurs in the waking state. In the waking state, the primary process is not wish fulfilling, as Freud believed, but functions as an inference making tool utilizing metaphor and metonymy. As such, rapid, unconscious primary process thinking is at the heart of our survival.

Jutta Kahl-Popp   Dr. Phil. Jutta Kahl-Popp, psychoanalyst (DPV, VAKJP) is in private practice; supervisor, training analyst; lecturer, psychoanalytic coaching and counseling; surveyor of German “Kassenärztliche Bundesvereinigung;” awarded by IPA in 2009 with “Psychoanalytic Training Today Award”; IPA-RTP fellow; scientific interests: clinical and conceptual issues of psychoanalysis; psychotherapy research; research of psychotherapists’ education; various publications.Lütjohannstr. 22, 24159 Kiel, Germany, Jutta.Kahl-Popp@t-online.de

In psychoanalytic training institutions, there is a pedagogical conflict inherent: The respective training/teaching generation of psychoanalysts regard their theoretical and clinical knowledge as learning goals for the next generation of psychoanalysts. If teaching goals and learning goals are merged together, teaching takes place mostly in a projective and possessive manner. From this perspective, supervision is probably the main place of transmitting the structural psychoanalytic superego-complex (Kahl-Popp 2005, 2007; Reeder, 2004), which can paralyze learning capacities and further development of the next generation of analysts.

To solve this pedagogical conflict it is necessary to abandon the paradigm fulfilling the targets of teaching/training analysts and supervisors. For this purpose, basic lines of a psychoanalytic concept of learning are described. The affinities between learning in psychoanalysis, psychoanalytic treatment, and learning in supervision are characterized. Symptoms, experiences of emotional discrepancies, and interactional dysfunctions are considered as demands of learning in both fields. Furthermore the answering interventions—interpretations, relational and supportive interventions or instructions—of psychoanalysts and supervisors will be investigated from the perspective of being helpful or not helpful for the learning capacities of patients and supervisees. A patient- and supervisee-centered psychoanalytic concept of evaluation is proposed. In this evaluation concept, the manifest and latent feedback of patients and supervisees, following directly to an intervention, is regarded as an important source for orientation, which will be needed to learn in psychoanalytic clinical practice and supervision.

It is illustrated how this evaluation concept can be used for research purposes to investigate the impact of supervision on learning psychoanalytic–psychotherapeutic competence.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue: Psychoanalysis and Evolution: The Tentative Connection

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Sociobiology, the study of animal behavior with applications to human beings, and psychoanalysis, the study of the mind with application to the biology of human beings, have been isolated from each other like children involved in parallel play. The special knowledge from both fields, which has been outside of each other’s reach, can be bridged by evolutionary principles based on the common origin of animals and humans that is influenced by natural selection of the body and mind. A controversy arose three decades ago that has become a catalyst toward greater use of evolutionary principles and a beginning integration of both fields.

The controversy was in response to an academic book written by Edward O. Wilson, an eminent Harvard University Professor. In 1975, Wilson produced an encyclopedic book on animal behavior entitled Sociobiology: A New Synthesis. Although under normal circumstances textbooks on evolution and animal behavior seldom become best sellers or arouse much media attention, Wilson’s tome was different. In the final chapter of the book, Wilson described how the latest advances in the study of animal behavior, particularly the insights of biologist Robert Trivers who introduced reciprocal altruism and Bill Hamilton who introduced game theory, might explain many aspects of human behavior. He provided biological explanations for a broad array of controversial topics including the differences between the sexes, human aggression, religion, homosexuality and xenophobia. He also predicted that it would not be long before the social sciences were subsumed with the biological science.

Wilson’s book provoked an uproar and launched what is now known as “the sociobiology debate” that raged in the 1970s and 1980s. The critics reacted to Wilson’s initial inroad to the connection of animal behavior and human existence accusing Wilson of supporting an exclusive genetic bias of human characteristics which in the past led to Social Darwinism, Nazism and Eugenics. (Laland and Brown, 2011, p. 3)

Richard Wagner: Grandiosity, Entitlement, and its Metastases

Frank Lachmann PHD

Frank Lachmann

Frank Lachmann   Frank M. Lachmann, Ph.D., is a member of the Founding Faculty of the Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity, New York, and Clinical Assistant Professor in the NYU Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis. He is author of Transforming Aggression and Transforming Narcissism: Reflections on Empathy, Humor, and Expectation. 140 Riverside Drive Apt. 1-O, New York, NY 10024, framlach@aol.com

Richard Wagner was a genius. About this there is little doubt among musicians and musicologists. It is also a judgment with which Wagner, himself, would have readily concurred. There was also little doubt among those who knew him that he was a scoundrel. As a genius, he felt entitled. The two-dimensionality of his character stands in sharp contrast to the complex, three-dimensional characters that populate his operas. However, his evil characters are all Jews, and his anti-Semitism reigned supreme in his life and art. His creativity died with him, but his grandiosity, entitlement, and anti-Semitism metastasized to his children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, and found a welcome home with Adolf Hitler. In this article, I describe Wagner’s early life, his near-death experience shortly after he was born, his recollections of his cold mother, his unclear paternity, and his self-aggrandizing autobiography in which he depicted himself as having had the childhood and parents that he felt would have befit the extraordinarily creative person he considered himself to be. Nevertheless, his impact on the musical world was revolutionary.

Rita Cahn LCSW

Rita Cahn

Rita Cahn   Rita Karuna Cahn, LCSW, is a psychotherapist in private practice in San Francisco. She is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of California San Francisco, and is on the supervising and teaching faculty of The Psychotherapy Institute, Berkeley. 322 Clement Street, San Francisco, CA 94118, ritakaruna@mac.com

This article traces my evolution as a political activist in relation to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict over the past decade, and describes the ways my activism has become integrated into my professional life. I discuss my journeys in Israel/Palestine with delegations of the Compassionate Listening Project, highlighting disturbing stories of injustice and abuse and inspiring stories of interfaith cooperation and nonviolent peace work. My focus is on the emotional impact of becoming the bearer of stories of unbearable human experience that I felt compelled to bring back and share. I reveal my struggles with continuing to speak and write publically about the injustice that I witnessed. In the course of standing up to both internal and external attacks on bearing witness, I have discovered a stronger therapeutic voice with my patients as well.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue: Analytic Lives in a Wounded World

Doris Brothers PHD

Doris Brothers

Doris Brothers  

In recent years, we have had to come to grips with a realization that earlier generations of analysts could more easily ignore: The world invades our consulting rooms. Continually bombarded by news reports from our radios, televisions, computers, and smartphones of calamitous events arising in every part of our shrinking planet, we cannot help but notice the societal context of our patients’ troubles. Nor can we fail to appreciate the futility of trying to tease apart their familial dramas from events occurring on the world stage.

The greater our distance from our mythic, blank-screen, authoritarian analytic predecessors, and the more we have come to view ourselves as flesh-and-blood, fallible, responsive, vulnerable individuals, the more clearly we see that our formative experiences contribute to the unfolding of our analytic relationships, at times as powerfully as those of our patients. Because our experiences, like theirs, were shaped by the larger social/cultural/political realm in which they are embedded, a deeper understanding of ourselves in the world—and the world in ourselves—seems likely to enhance our therapeutic effectiveness.

This issue is dedicated to just this project. It investigates how living in a world scarred by violence, upheaval, and injustice influences the ways in which analysts think and feel and work.

There can be little doubt that grievous circumstances in their homelands profoundly affected the lives and theories of our psychoanalytic pioneers. Freud is no exception. Leaving little room for doubt that anti-Semitism infiltrated many aspects of Freud’s life and thought, Peter Gay (1988), his distinguished biographer, writes: “He abandoned the dubious privilege of belonging, sensing that his isolation would serve him well” (p. 27). The one-person orientation of Freudian drive theory may well reflect the defiant self-sufficiency Freud developed in the face of rejection and contempt (Brothers and Lewis, 2012). Aron and Starr (2013) document the profound effects of anti-Semitism on psychoanalysis, contending, for example, that the polarities of activity-passivity, femininity-masculinity, religious belief-science that characterize psychoanalysis reflect Freud’s efforts to gain universal acceptance for his theory.

[[RunningHead]]

Notes on “Confusion of Tongues” by S. Ferenczi

M. W.

M. W.

M. W.  

I admire his self-criticism. He [Ferenczi] saw that in his attempt to help his patients with their trauma head-on, he was in fact causing them considerable pain without a fundamental change in their condition. His well-intentioned efforts to deal consciously with their problem were being experienced by them as an assault. The difficulty of understanding the structurally damaged patient is made more so in that where once it may have seemed adequate for a therapist to have been analyzed right down to the rock bottom, it has now become necessary for the rock bottom rock itself to become known to them to help the patient. The changes in Ferenczi’s attitude toward his patients—a 180° change—revealing his flaws to them had to have been validated by him (I would like to think) by how he felt when he first began doing it. This willingness on his part to set aside preconceived concepts and ideas about analysis and become a mother to his child-patients must have cost him dearly, considering the time of day and the orthodoxy opposing it. Today it is the infant-patient who needs to be nurtured and understood.

In his casual matter of fact presentation of sexual abuse midway through the paper, what appears at face to be a presentation of an already accepted premise was in fact a bombshell. The opening shots aimed at a crime that is rapidly proving to be the scandal of our century.

When it comes to incest, I feel certain that there is no pathology in tenderness (itself), which Ferenczi links in a way to the erotic that somehow can become incestuous. Having never ever experienced tenderness from my mother until I was sixty, I protest his extrapolation of the infant’s need for the breast and the mother’s adaptation on primal grounds! Tenderness would no longer be considered tender when it becomes excited. (One is cool and the other is feverish.) The erotic is still not sexual. I believe there are clear demarcations in the mother–infant relationship. There is confusion here between tenderness and excitement and quietude and “passion” on the part of the infant-child when the child has had to create two mothers in order to account for it. (Sex, as in sexuality, is an adult concept and is unknown to the infant.)

Paolo Stramba-Badiale

Paolo Stramba-Badiale   Dr. Stramba-Badiale is Psychoanalyst; Faculty and Training Analyst, ISIPSé (Institute of Specialization in Psychoanalytic Self Psychology and Relational Psychoanalysis); Member IAPSP and IARPP; and Member of the Council of IAPSP, Milan, Rome, Italy. Veronica, a thirty-year-old woman who worked as a mid-level manager for a software company, began her analysis in October ten years ago. I was forty-two at the time.

She was referred to me by her father, an engineer whom I had met a few years before at a conference on psychoanalysis. On that occasion, her father had heard me give a talk on daydreaming and it occurred to him at that particular moment that his former analyst had recommended my name to him years ago to analyze his daughter.

Twenty years earlier, Veronica’s father had begun psychotherapy after experiencing episodes of fragmentation and dissociation, which resulted in him being admitted to a psychiatric hospital several times. Thanks to the successful analysis, which brought him great psychological relief, he then developed a genuine cultural interest in psychoanalysis.

He therefore suggested to his daughter that she begin psychotherapy herself, which Veronica decided to do at the age of twenty. However, this first attempt proved unsuccessful, due to the difficulties she encountered in her relationships with others and her general state of insecurity. Veronica started group therapy, but found it difficult to relate to. As a consequence, she began having doubts about psychological treatment in general, and feeling that she was not suited for it. She later told me that she had also had difficulty with the analyst, whom she considered to be too judgmental and thorough in his approach, so much so that she experienced an almost physical discomfort during the few sessions she attended.

In the course of our initial interview, I could not help but to compare the physical appearance of this tall, voluptuous woman in her early thirties with that of her father, whom I remembered as being rather short and pudgy. She had Mediterranean features and a dignity about her that is distinctive of young women from well-to-do families who are accustomed to the comforts of a cushioned existence. I noticed her elegant outfits and sophisticated accessories, which I actually found to be somewhat excessive and which made her look “older”.

Hanne Strømme

Hanne Strømme

Hanne Strømme   Hanne Strømme is Associate Professor, Department of Psychology, at the University of Oslo. Department of Psychology, University of Oslo, P.O. Box 1094, Blindern, Oslo, 0317, Norway, hanne.stromme@psykologi.uio.no

This is a qualitative study of the supervision processes of two trainee clinical psychologists who conduct their first intensive psychodynamic therapy. The study questions whether the trainees’ degree of disclosure of feelings toward their supervisors to the supervisor was influenced by the evoked relational scenarios in them. The trainees had one patient each, two sessions a week for ten months, with supervision weekly. The study includes three process interviews with the trainees during the supervision, and a fourth, follow-up interview one year later. Additionally, an independent evaluation of their therapist competence is included, based on the fifth last therapy session. The two supervision processes are first presented separately. Hypotheses of relational scenarios evoked in the trainees toward their supervisors are inferred. It is concluded that these relational scenarios may have influenced the degree of these trainees’ disclosure of negative feelings toward their supervisors. Supervisors are recommended to be particularly sensitive to which relational scenarios may be evoked in novice trainees in the supervision relationship.

Never Ever Stop Learning More About Supervision is a very adequate title for this gathering of excellent articles on supervision, as well as it is a very proper motto for Imre Szecsödy’s extraordinary and tireless contributions for the current understanding of this complex process that is at the very core of analytic training. As in so many fields of human activity, there are a few persons who embrace an idea, a cause, an ideology, a mission, and dedicate the best of their efforts to bring more light, or effectiveness to this cause; international psychoanalysis owes to Imre and his work a more clear, objective and research-oriented view on the fascinating activity that is psychoanalytic supervision.

In my view, the articles presented here show the many dilemmas, complexities, and controversies on analytic supervision. For the one side, we see nowadays a consistent search for objectivity and of measurable learning objectives, as the articles from Moga and Cabaniss, and Watkins and Scaturo clearly suggest. Moga and Cabaniss present a plea for clearly delineated measurable learning objectives and show how this can be used and its relevance for analytic training.

In his delineation of guidelines for conducting psychoanalytic treatment, Sigmund Freud (1912) explicitly declared that what he was recommending suited his character and that others might find their own ways of acting upon these principles. Before the reader winces and begins to question the veracity of my statement, allow me to quote the master himself.

The technical rules which I am putting forward here have been arrived at from my own experience in the course of many years … I must, however, make it clear that what I’m asserting is that this technique is the only one suited to my individuality; I do not venture to deny that a physician quite differently constituted might find himself driven to adopt a different attitude to his patients and to the task before him. (p. 111)

Despite Freud’s acknowledgment that different psychoanalysts might be differently constituted and despite his clear permission for others to be innovative and tailor the therapeutic technique to their personal styles, most practitioners of psychoanalysis took the opposite path. They clung to his guidelines and assiduously attempted to craft a proper or standard or mainstream or classical technique.

Kurt Eissler’s (1953) concept of parameters, i.e.. temporary and clinical need-based departures from a standard technique, strengthened the belief—widely-held at that time—that a correct way of conducting psychoanalysis did exist. Heinz Hartmann’s (1960) pronouncement that “the analytic therapy is a kind of technology” (p. 21) put a further seal of dignity on the elimination of subjectivity, variation, and nuance from our clinical enterprise. The fact that variations in the character styles (e.g., brooding, sunny, methodical, playful) of individual analysts could impact upon their manner of practice was banished from the profession’s awareness.

Privately, however, no one believed that all analysts worked alike. Certainly the cautious Anna Freud, the incisive Melanie Klein, and the playful Donald Winnicott were not the same in their clinical interventions. To be sure, all three subscribed to the “trio of guideposts” (Pine, 1997, p. 13) of anonymity, abstinence, and neutrality but, in the end, they worked quite differently. 204

Different narratives of memory are discussed: the collective, cultural discourse of memory in Germany today; autobiographical memory among Germans and those of German descent; and the impact of history and the role of memory in the clinical situation. Personal experience and its role in the analytic setting is examined within the context of cultural discourses that shape collective and autobiographical memory. The author draws on his experience as a psychoanalyst of German descent, and as a so-called third-generation German. Analytic work with second and third generation Holocaust survivors is discussed. Emphasis is placed on the emotional contexts of memory, and on affect states, such as shame, which challenge and complicate the navigation of history and memory, particularly in analytic interactions.

Kenneth Israelstam

Kenneth Israelstam

Kenneth Israelstam   Dr. Israelstam is Training Analyst and Member of the Australian Psychoanalytical Society; Chair of the Sydney Branch of the Australian Psychoanalytical Society; and Member of the International Psychoanalytic Society. 5 Marian, Killara, NSW 2075, Australia, kenisraelstam@optusnet.com.au

It is heartwarming to be able to immerse myself in such enriching articles that contribute to psychoanalysis’ much-needed and growing emphasis, on being able to understand, expand, and articulate the process of analytic supervision. I am especially pleased to find that these articles cover collectively what are, for me, the central core issues that require further exploration: a conceptual framework of education; the relationship between theory and practice of psychoanalysis and supervision; relating candidate learning objectives to goals of supervision; and the how-to of practice, and, very important, research.

The analytic model based on the wise elders’ stance of, I know, I teach, you learn, has prevailed now for too long. This collection of articles has certainly helped to lead readers away from what has essentially been, a deterministic, ordered, and knowing framework, toward I inspire, stimulate, influence; you learn, essentially a postmodern view, where immediacy, ambiguity, and doubt are valued.

I begin with Gábor Szőnyi’s article. Without offering his direct opinion, Szőnyi describes the Budapest model of supervision, where the analyst provides a dual function of analyst and supervisor. He points out that this practice of the analysts’ dual roles continued until after WWII, when the Hungarian Society joined the International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA) and, thereby, (with reluctance) were obliged to abide by their standards of separate roles for analysis and supervision.

There is nothing like a Ferenczian-type controversy to awaken our thinking about theory and practice of supervision. It was Gregory Bateson who stated, “Information is a difference” (Bateson, 1972). Without a continual flow of new information and ideas, we are destined to remain stagnant and soon become outmoded!

Szőnyi describes variations on this theme, such as initiating supervision during the termination phase, using one of three sessions per week, and conducting on the couch versus face-to-face. In an open-minded way, he goes on to describe the pros and cons of the earlier Budapest model versus the IPA’s framework that requires separate analysts and supervisors.

This article begins with Freud’s struggles in dealing with the concept of transference. His struggles were particularly acute with certain types of narcissistic patients. The view presented is that Freud, in some ways, was prototypic of the type of struggles that contemporary analysts have in allowing transference manifestations to effloresce. Kohut is seen as advancing the struggle and setting a new boundary for analyzability that allowed analysts to begin to move into the patient’s world. Eva Papiasvili

Eva Papiasvili   Eva Dubska Papiasvili, Ph.D., ABPP is Supervising Faculty, Doctoral Program in Clinical Psychology, Columbia University; Training and Supervising Analyst, Former Executive Director and Dean, Postgraduate Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; and Teaching and Supervising Faculty, Object Relations Institute. 136 East 55th Street, New York, NY, 10022, Eva.papiasvili@gmail.com

The underreporting of childhood traumatic etiology of the later onset chronic posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) of our present day Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM IV: APA 1994) has complex societal-cultural, as well as unconscious, reasons, complexities of which are written already into the original Ferenczi’s concept of Identification with the Aggressor, as corroborated by the contemporary dynamic developmental neuroscience. Ferenczi’s is the pathogenic sequence (unlike Anna Freud’s later concept of the same name) resulting in the Identification with the Aggressor including the Confusion of Tongues between the adult abuser and the abused child, which results in a layered configuration of posttraumatic identifications of the Wise Child and the Identification with the Aggressor. The clinical vignette illustrates the dynamic complexity of the overall Identification with the Aggressor, with the Confusion of Tongues acquiring additional internalized form through perceptual–affective cross-modal (con)fusion: while looking in the mirror, the patient saw part of his face missing. The technical armamentarium of a flexible interpsychic/intropsychic model of psychoanalytic work with enactments is employed and illustrated in detail as a contemporary equivalent of Ferenczi’s active elastic psychoanalytic technique.

In this article we suggest that current controversies around the psychoanalytic concepts of narcissism, omnipotence, specialness, and so forth derive from reliance on a single-track developmental model. A single-track model, used implicitly or explicitly by almost all psychoanalytic theorists, posits that normal infants and children function in ways that would be considered pathological in later life. This way of thinking is contradicted by modern infant and developmental research. Additionally, it contradicts common-sense experience and is, therefore, not a useful model for parenting. On the other hand, Freud and many other writers also posited a dual-track model, which simultaneously allows for both healthy and pathological choices throughout life. In this article, we describe some of the ways in which a dual-track model, which we have elaborated as two systems of self-regulation, can be usefully applied to theory, technique, and applications with all those involved with children.

This foray into largely uncharted psychoanalytic territory addresses Ron Bodansky’s question about what siblings have to do with psychological survival and healing in situations of extreme developmental trauma. This article speculates that, except when psychological organization has been destroyed at an age when before sibling connections become relevant—see “Fear of Breakdown” (Winnicott, 1974)—siblings can both transmit timeless intergenerational trauma within a generation, and contribute to the survival of such damage.
